title: MECM · Client and Enterprise Operations
description: Manage test clients, collections, software, heartbeat discovery, health and compliance.
baseline: Configuration Manager current branch · MECM01 · lab.example.test
prerequisite: Finish the MECM install and site configuration labs first. Keep DC01, SQL01, MECM01 and one practice member-server client ready. Check the supported OS/SQL matrix for your evaluation release.
supplies: A working evaluation primary site and console with the required management/distribution roles.
An approved lab.example.test test client; do not use a domain controller as the pilot.
A trusted, licensed test MSI and administrative permission inside your private lab.

lessons.description: Connect one practice lab.example.test member server to your lab site and prove that its client is managed.
lessons.what: Connect one practice lab.example.test member server to your lab site and prove that its client is managed.

steps.title: Check the site before adding a client
actions: Open the Configuration Manager console on MECM01. Select Administration → Site Configuration → Sites.
Write down the actual three-character site code shown for your primary site; use that value wherever this class says your site code.
Select Monitoring → System Status → Site Status. Resolve critical role failures before continuing.
steps.expected: The intended primary site is listed and its management point and distribution point are available.

breakdown.meaning: A short label identifies the site your client belongs to. Do not guess it from the server name.

steps.title: Prepare the practice client
actions: Use APP01 only if it is a practice member server and you can change it safely. Do not use either domain controller as your first client.
Open Start → Windows PowerShell. Run hostname, then open System → About and confirm the device is joined to lab.example.test.
Check that APP01 uses the lab DNS server and can resolve MECM01.lab.example.test. Confirm the ports required by your site design rather than disabling the firewall.
steps.expected: APP01 is a domain member, its name is recorded, and MECM01 resolves to the intended private address.

breakdown.meaning: This is the computer that receives software and reports health; MECM01 manages it.

screenshot.title: Interface reference: Windows Terminal · PowerShell profile and prompt
screenshot.instructions: Orientation reference for the named application, not a capture of every action in this step. Follow the written instructions and expected result; original example values and versions may differ.

steps.title: Install the client from the site share
actions: Open File Explorer. In its address bar enter \\MECM01.lab.example.test\SMS_<your site code>\Client, replacing the entire <your site code> text with the code you recorded.
Copy that Client folder to C:\Lab\CMClient on APP01. Open Windows PowerShell as administrator on APP01.

Run C:\Lab\CMClient\ccmsetup.exe /mp:MECM01.lab.example.test SMSSITECODE=<your site code>, replacing the placeholder before pressing Enter. Use this only for the lab site configured for HTTP/enhanced HTTP; a PKI HTTPS site needs its documented certificate options.
Open C:\Windows\ccmsetup\Logs\ccmsetup.log with CMTrace from the site tools, or Notepad. Wait for ccmsetup to finish; a return code of 0 indicates successful setup.
steps.expected: The client installation finishes successfully and Control Panel includes Configuration Manager.

breakdown.meaning: The installer puts the management client on APP01. The site code assigns it to your existing lab site.

steps.title: Confirm the client reports to the console
actions: Select Assets and Compliance → Devices. Find APP01. Allow time for registration and discovery; refresh the view.
Check the Client column and site assignment. If the device needs approval under your site policy, review its identity and approve only this known lab device.
On APP01 open Control Panel → Configuration Manager → Actions. Select Machine Policy Retrieval & Evaluation Cycle → Run Now.
steps.expected: APP01 appears with Client = Yes and the intended site code. A policy request is visible in its PolicyAgent.log.

breakdown.meaning: An entry in Devices alone is not proof that client installation succeeded; check Client = Yes and the logs.

lessons.title: Create Pilot and Rollout Device Collections
lessons.description: Create a small pilot collection and a separate rollout collection so you can target changes deliberately.
lessons.what: Create a small pilot collection and a separate rollout collection so you can target changes deliberately.
lessons.why: A collection is your target list. Keeping pilot and rollout lists separate helps prevent accidental broad deployments.

steps.title: Create the pilot collection
actions: Select Assets and Compliance → Device Collections. Right-click Device Collections → Create Device Collection.
Enter LAB-Pilot-Devices. Select Browse beside Limiting collection, choose All Systems, then select Next.
On Membership Rules select Add Rule → Direct Rule. Follow the wizard, search Name for APP01, and select only the verified APP01 device.
Finish both wizards. Leave recurring schedules at the lab default; do not enable frequent incremental updates for every collection.
steps.expected: LAB-Pilot-Devices exists with a direct membership rule for APP01.

breakdown.meaning: All Systems is only the membership boundary here. It is not the collection we will deploy software to.

steps.title: Check the actual members
actions: Right-click LAB-Pilot-Devices → Update Membership. Wait for evaluation, then select Refresh.
Right-click the collection → Show Members. Check every row.
Confirm APP01 is present and DC01/DC02 are absent. If an unexpected device appears, fix the membership rule before creating any deployment.
steps.expected: Only the intended practice pilot device is a member.

breakdown.meaning: The console calculates which devices belong to the collection; this can take time.

steps.title: Create a rollout collection without deploying yet
actions: Create another device collection named LAB-Rollout-Devices, also limited by All Systems.
Keep it empty until you have another approved practice client. Do not add domain controllers to make the lab look complete.
Open each collection’s Properties → Membership Rules and record which devices each rule selects.
steps.expected: Two separately named collections exist; the rollout collection is empty or contains only approved additional test devices.

breakdown.meaning: You test a change on the small pilot, check the result, and only then choose whether to expand it.

steps.title: Stage a small, trusted MSI
actions: Download a currently supported Windows MSI from its software publisher, such as the enterprise MSI for a free editor. Check its license and published checksum or signature.
Create a read-only application source share for this lab, for example \\MECM01.lab.example.test\LabSources\Apps\Editor. Store the MSI there.
Grant the site server computer account read access to the source, plus the administrators who maintain it. Keep ordinary client users from changing installer files.
steps.expected: The verified MSI is reachable by the site server through its UNC path.

breakdown.meaning: These are the original installer files that Configuration Manager copies to its distribution point.

steps.title: Create the MSI application and inspect detection
actions: Select Software Library → Application Management → Applications. Right-click Applications → Create Application.
Choose Automatically detect information about this application from installation files. Select Windows Installer (*.msi file), then browse to the UNC path of your MSI.
Review the imported application name and version. Complete the wizard. Open the application’s Deployment Types, then its MSI deployment type → Properties.
Review Programs for install/uninstall commands, Detection Method for the MSI product code, and User Experience for the intended install context. Do not copy a product code from another application.
steps.expected: One application exists with the actual MSI identity, install/uninstall commands and detection rule.

breakdown.meaning: This tells the client how to check whether the software is already installed. A wrong rule can make successful installs look failed.

steps.title: Send content to the distribution point
actions: Right-click the application → Distribute Content. Select the lab distribution point and finish.
Open Monitoring → Distribution Status → Content Status. Select the application and open View Status.
Wait until content is successfully distributed. Investigate errors before deploying.
steps.expected: Content Status shows success for the intended lab distribution point.

breakdown.meaning: This server stores the installer that the client will download.

steps.title: Offer the application only to the pilot
actions: Right-click the application → Deploy. Choose LAB-Pilot-Devices and verify its membership before selecting Next.
Select the lab distribution point. Set Action = Install and Purpose = Available. Complete the remaining wizard pages after reviewing the settings.
On APP01 request machine policy from Control Panel → Configuration Manager → Actions. Open Start → Software Center → Applications. Select the test application → Install.
steps.expected: The application appears in Software Center on APP01 and installs successfully; it was not assigned to All Systems.

breakdown.meaning: The learner chooses Install in Software Center. Required would enforce an installation schedule.

steps.title: Verify installation, then test removal
actions: Open the application and check its version. In MECM Monitoring → Deployments, select the deployment and review its client status.

On APP01 open Software Center → Applications → the test application. Select Uninstall when offered, then confirm it is removed. If unavailable, review the application’s configured uninstall command and deployment rules before retrying.
For failures check C:\Windows\CCM\Logs\AppDiscovery.log, AppIntentEval.log and AppEnforce.log. Remove or retire the pilot deployment when your exercise is complete.
steps.expected: The application installs, opens, and uninstalls on APP01, with matching client logs and deployment status.

breakdown.meaning: Check the actual program and the client logs; the console may take time to receive the latest status.

lessons.title: Check Heartbeat Discovery and Client Health
lessons.description: Send a heartbeat from APP01 and use client checks and logs to investigate a device that stops reporting.
lessons.what: Send a heartbeat from APP01 and use client checks and logs to investigate a device that stops reporting.
lessons.why: Heartbeat discovery refreshes a device record. It is not a live ping and does not prove that applications or Windows are healthy.

steps.title: Review the heartbeat schedule
actions: Select Administration → Hierarchy Configuration → Discovery Methods.
Open Heartbeat Discovery → Properties. Check whether it is enabled and record the schedule already configured.
Keep the existing lab schedule unless you have a specific reason to change it. Do not confuse Heartbeat Discovery with Active Directory System Discovery.
steps.expected: You can identify the enabled state and actual heartbeat schedule.

breakdown.meaning: A client periodically sends a discovery record so the site can refresh information about it.

steps.title: Request one heartbeat on APP01
actions: Open Control Panel → Configuration Manager → Actions. Select Discovery Data Collection Cycle → Run Now.
Open C:\Windows\CCM\Logs\InventoryAgent.log with CMTrace. Find entries for the discovery cycle you just requested.
Back in the console, open APP01’s discovery information and compare its latest discovery time after processing. Allow time for the site to update.
steps.expected: The client log records the requested cycle and the discovery record later refreshes.

breakdown.meaning: This asks the client to send its record now instead of waiting for the next scheduled heartbeat.

steps.title: Read the client health checks
actions: Select Monitoring → Client Status → Client Check, then review Client Activity. Limit investigation to your pilot devices.
On APP01 check that the SMS Agent Host service (CcmExec) is running. Open C:\Windows\CCM\Logs\CcmEval.log and review the latest client evaluation.

If policy or health fails, also check ClientIDManagerStartup.log, CcmMessaging.log and PolicyAgent.log for the matching time. Check DNS, service state and the configured management point before considering a repair.
steps.expected: You can distinguish a recent heartbeat, an active client, and a passed or failed client evaluation.

breakdown.meaning: Client evaluation checks the management client itself. It is different from application health or operating-system patch compliance.

steps.title: Rehearse a brief client outage safely
actions: Use only the practice APP01 client. Record its service state, then open Services and stop SMS Agent Host briefly. Do not stop the management services on MECM01.
Observe that an immediate green console status can be stale. Record the time; do not wait days for inactivity thresholds just to finish the lab.
Start SMS Agent Host again. Request machine policy and confirm new entries in PolicyAgent.log. Compare the next client health evaluation.
steps.expected: APP01’s client service is restored and requests policy again; you can explain why a green console icon was not a live health probe.

breakdown.meaning: Use a specific test for a specific question: service state for the agent, a policy request for management communication, and an application test for the app.

lessons.description: Check that a harmless lab registry value exists, deploy the check to the pilot, and observe compliant and noncompliant results.
lessons.what: Check that a harmless lab registry value exists, deploy the check to the pilot, and observe compliant and noncompliant results.
lessons.why: A compliance starting point compares a device with a rule. Start with a check-only rule before enabling automatic changes.

steps.title: Create a harmless setting on the pilot
actions: Open Windows PowerShell as administrator on APP01. Run New-Item -Path HKLM:\SOFTWARE\CloudSeamLab -Force.
Run New-ItemProperty -Path HKLM:\SOFTWARE\CloudSeamLab -Name LabReady -PropertyType String -Value Yes -Force.
Open Registry Editor and verify HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\CloudSeamLab contains the LabReady string set to Yes. Do not change other keys.
steps.expected: The practice lab value exists on APP01.

breakdown.meaning: This is a harmless practice value. It is not a Microsoft security recommendation or proof of endpoint security.

screenshot.title: Interface reference: Windows Terminal · PowerShell profile and prompt
screenshot.instructions: Orientation reference for the named application, not a capture of every action in this step. Follow the written instructions and expected result; original example values and versions may differ.

steps.title: Define the configuration item
actions: Select Assets and Compliance → Compliance Settings → Configuration Items → Create Configuration Item.
Name it LAB-Registry-Readiness and choose a Windows desktop/server custom configuration item. Select the Windows versions used by your client.
Add a Registry value setting with data type String: hive HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, key SOFTWARE\CloudSeamLab, value LabReady. Choose the 64-bit registry view for this x64 lab client.
Add a compliance rule that the value Equals Yes, and report noncompliance if the value is missing. Leave remediation disabled.
steps.expected: The item checks the exact lab value and does not automatically change a device.

breakdown.meaning: A single check describes a setting and the value you expect to find.

screenshot.title: Interface reference: Include configured baselines in compliance policy assessment condition
screenshot.instructions: Orientation reference for the named application, not a capture of every action in this step. Follow the written instructions and expected result; original example values and versions may differ.

steps.title: Deploy the baseline to the pilot
actions: Select Compliance Settings → Configuration Baselines → Create Configuration Baseline. Name it LAB-Pilot-Readiness.
Add the configuration item you just created. Deploy the starting point only to LAB-Pilot-Devices. Leave remediation unchecked and choose a reasonable lab evaluation schedule.
On APP01 request machine policy. Open Control Panel → Configuration Manager → Configurations. When the starting point arrives, select it and choose Evaluate, then View Report.
steps.expected: The pilot evaluates the starting point as compliant while LabReady equals Yes.

breakdown.meaning: A starting point bundles the checks you want a target collection to evaluate.

screenshot.title: Interface reference: Configuration Baseline Properties dialog box
screenshot.instructions: Orientation reference for the named application, not a capture of every action in this step. Follow the written instructions and expected result; original example values and versions may differ.

steps.title: Prove the rule detects a mismatch
actions: On APP01 change only the practice LabReady string from Yes to No. Evaluate the starting point again and view its report.
Confirm the starting point reports noncompliance. Change LabReady back to Yes, evaluate again, and confirm compliance.
Record both results. When finished, remove the lab starting point deployment before deleting the practice registry key; leave unrelated settings alone.
steps.expected: The same starting point reports noncompliance for No and compliance for Yes, without remediation.

breakdown.meaning: The actual value does not match your rule. It does not automatically mean the device has malware.

steps.title: Review site and component health
actions: Open Monitoring → System Status → Site Status and Component Status.
For a warning or critical component, right-click it → Show Messages and choose the matching severity and time range.
Record the component, time and message ID. Do not reset counts merely to make the display green.

breakdown.meaning: A message gives saved result about a component; its timestamp matters when deciding whether the issue is current.

steps.title: Check content and deployment failures
actions: Open Monitoring → Distribution Status → Content Status. Investigate failed or in-progress pilot content.
Open Monitoring → Deployments. Select your pilot deployment and compare success, in-progress and error states with APP01 client logs.
Open Monitoring → Client Status and record inactive or failed client checks. Keep hardware inventory and software inventory separate from compliance results.
steps.expected: The daily note separates content delivery, application results and client health.

breakdown.meaning: A healthy site role does not prove every application installed. Check each stage of the delivery path.

steps.title: Review maintenance and recovery safely
actions: Select Administration → Site Configuration → Sites. Open Site Maintenance and review the existing tasks without changing retention values blindly.
Review whether Backup Site Server is configured and where it writes. Check its latest success saved result and the independent SQL/site recovery plan.
Document the recovery location and a planned restore-test date. Do not restore or revert a domain-joined site server just to test a daily checklist.
steps.expected: You can name the backup saved result and recovery owner, plus any unresolved health issue.

breakdown.meaning: A scheduled task is not proof of a usable backup. A separate, planned recovery test is needed.
